LayerEditor flips that workflow. The resulting images retained > 90 % of the original aesthetic quality, confirming that the RGBA masks preserve semantic integrity across domains. Open‑Source Impact The model’s weights, inference script, and a Python SDK landed on Hugging Face on October 10 2026 . Within 48 hours the repository amassed 182 up‑votes, 1.4 M downloads, and 12 k unique API keys . The community already contributed three plugins: Figma LayerStudio – real‑time layer insertion. Photoshop LayerBridge – automatic PSD export. Unity AssetInjector – runtime texture replacement. These extensions prove that the Apache 2.0 license fuels rapid ecosystem growth, while the commercial LayerEditor‑Pro API targets enterprises that need SLA‑grade uptime and usage analytics. 4. Competitive Landscape System Core Method Layer Output Release 2026 Strengths Weaknesses LayerEditor Compositional Edit‑Prior Distillation (dual‑stage diffusion + transformer) Native RGBA per semantic region Oct 17 2026 Joint optimization guarantees layer fidelity; 2× faster than test‑time optimization; open‑source SDK Requires A100‑class hardware for optimal speed MRT – Masked Region Transformer Masked‑region diffusion trained on region‑level masks Binary masks only (no color channel) May 2026 Handles up to 10 regions; strong segmentation accuracy No color/alpha; extra compositing step InstructEdit+ (OpenAI) Instruction‑conditioned diffusion with post‑hoc CLIP‑based mask extraction No built‑in layers; masks derived after edit Sep 2026 Large instruction dataset; robust text understanding Mask quality drops 30 % on fine‑grained objects; extra inference pass Adobe Sensei LayerGen Proprietary transformer that predicts layer masks from user strokes Masks only, no RGBA Aug 2026 (beta) Tight Photoshop integration Closed source; limited to Adobe ecosystem; slower (≈ 1.4 s per edit) Stable Diffusion XL + ControlNet ControlNet guides diffusion with external edge maps; user supplies masks Relies on user‑provided masks Jun 2026 Flexible control signals; strong community support No automatic layer extraction; manual mask creation required LayerEditor is the only system that simultaneously learns to edit and to produce full RGBA layers in a single forward pass . Competitors either sacrifice color fidelity, require extra post‑processing, or lock the workflow inside a single vendor’s UI. 5. Risks and Mitigation Risk Why it matters Mitigation Compute accessibility – 1.2 B‑parameter model runs best on A100‑80 GB GPUs. Small studios may see latency > 3 s per edit. An 8‑bit quantized variant runs on RTX 3080‑Ti with only a 1.6× slowdown. Enterprises can also off‑load to the LayerEditor‑Pro cloud endpoint (auto‑scaling, pay‑as‑you‑go). Semantic drift in layer reuse – Extreme style mismatches can cause halo artifacts. Reusing a pastel neon layer on a gritty cyberpunk scene may look off‑brand. The SDK ships a LayerBlend utility (lightweight style‑transfer) and a “refine layer” flag that triggers a brief 10‑step diffusion focused on the selected mask. Data‑privacy – Public endpoint stores prompt‑image pairs for analytics. Proprietary brand assets could be unintentionally exposed. Commercial API offers on‑premise inference containers (Docker) and supports private fine‑tuning so firms can keep brand‑specific priors behind their firewall. Licensing fragmentation – Dual‑license (Apache 2.0 vs. commercial) can confuse developers. Mixing open‑source SDK calls with paid API endpoints may violate terms. Documentation includes a license matrix and a code‑generation wizard that tags each function with its appropriate license. The community already built a license‑aware CI pipeline that blocks prohibited mixes. 6. Outlook: Where Layers Lead the Industry LayerEditor’s launch marks the first practical realization of non‑destructive AI editing at scale. The ripple effects will likely manifest in three arenas: Design systems as layer libraries – Brands can curate reusable AI‑generated layers (e.g., “summer‑light flare,” “brand‑color accent”) that developers embed directly into web‑apps, turning generative AI into a true component library. Dynamic asset pipelines – Game studios can feed a base texture into LayerEditor, request “add moss patches,” and then reuse the moss layer across dozens of 3D models, dramatically shrinking texture‑authoring cycles. Automated marketing at scale – Platforms like Canva will let non‑designers pick a “brand palette layer” that automatically recolors all text, icons, and backgrounds, guaranteeing brand compliance without manual checks. If the early adopters’ productivity gains hold up, we can expect a 30‑40 % reduction in average creative turnaround time across advertising, UI/UX, and gaming sectors by 2028. Companies that embed LayerEditor into their pipelines today will capture that efficiency head‑start; late entrants may need to retrofit legacy assets or purchase third‑party layer marketplaces. 7. Closing Thoughts LayerEditor does not merely add a new button to the diffusion toolbox; it re‑architects the relationship between instruction, image, and mask . By treating layers as first‑class citizens, the system aligns AI output with the long‑established design principle of non‑destructive editing . The data speak clearly: higher fidelity, faster inference, and measurable workflow savings. The ecosystem already shows momentum, with plugins for the industry’s biggest design platforms and a cloud API that scales on demand. Nevertheless, teams must plan for compute costs, potential style drift, and licensing nuances. Those who address these challenges early will unlock a new class of reusable, AI‑generated assets that accelerate creative cycles across the board. Bottom line: October 2026 introduced a tool that finally bridges the gap between generative AI’s visual power and designers’ need for editable layers. In a world where speed to market decides success, LayerEditor gives creators the modular building blocks they have been waiting for . Key Stats 0.94 SSIM on Precise Local Manipulation (12 % over prior state‑of‑the‑art). > 90 % perceptual quality retained when reusing layers across unrelated images. 0.8 s per 512×512 edit on A100‑80 GB (≈ 2× faster than test‑time optimization baselines). 35 % reduction in manual masking effort reported by WPP, Publicis, and Dentsu pilots. Author’s note: I tested LayerEditor on a personal project (adding a vintage filter to a family portrait). The system produced a clean “filter” layer that I could toggle, edit opacity, and export to a GIF. The experience felt like working with Photoshop’s adjustment layers—only it was generated in seconds.

  • Layer‑reconstruction loss – pixel‑wise L2 between generated RGBA layers and ground‑truth masks.

items.title: YamRail: Treating LLMs as Heavy Machinery, Gated by Human Authority
items.summary: 1. Verification over Speculation I built an AI system that rigorously separates what can be confirmed with solid technical evidence, what remains mere speculation, and what cannot be concluded beyond a certain point. 2. Try the Public Beta Live Demo: https://yamrail.ai/kyk-cf/?presentation_language=en Please try the KYK public beta. If possible, I would like you to test its limits with tough, ambiguous, and demanding tasks. Note: I am not a native English speaker. Please share your thoughts in writing so we can maintain a clear, verifiable record. 3. LLMs as Heavy Machinery, Not Peers Today's Frontier AI narrative seems obsessed with the idea that humans and LLMs can stand shoulder to shoulder as peers. I disagree. An LLM is, at its core, heavy machinery for excavating knowledge . To operate safely alongside humans, it demands industrial-grade safety measures—just as a real-world construction site requires safety fences, lockouts, and strict permission boundaries to keep human workers out of hazardous zones. Blueprints: Mechanisms that compel the model to strictly follow human-defined specifications. Test Procedures: Standardized suites to verify output quality deterministically. Verified Inspection Records: Evidence-based logs that isolate exactly what humans need to inspect and verify. Without these explicit boundaries, LLMs will readily build elaborate castles nobody asked for. LLMs are inherently lazy, arrogant, and yet surprisingly patient. 4. The Real Problem: Approval Fatigue I am looking for architectural feedback. Where should human approval points and authority boundaries be placed? The output generated by LLMs can look deceptively flawless, yet conceal a single line capable of catastrophic failure. It is smooth and polished— like a razor blade hidden beneath a layer of cream. One naive engineering approach is to force the LLM to request approval at every single micro-step. But that is unworkable in production; it simply induces approval fatigue . It is like being required to call the bakery for permission before every single bite of cake. Nobody can build systems that way. As an initial prototype, I have implemented this workflow. Moving forward, I want to foster open discussion around standardizing these validation frameworks. items.title: How I Predict the Future: Gut Instinct, Verification, and Building
items.summary: I've noticed something interesting about the way I think about technology. Sometimes, I get a gut feeling about how something should work, how a product could evolve, or how people's relationship with technology might change. I don't always have a detailed explanation for it immediately. Sometimes, it's just an idea that feels worth exploring. But I don't stop at the feeling. I follow my intuition with verification. It Starts With a Gut Feeling Some ideas arrive before I have consciously analyzed every detail. Before AI-assisted interviews became a widely discussed topic, I supported the idea that candidates should be allowed to use AI during interviews. I had also explored the idea of modular, pluggable user interfaces before intelligent UIs became a more prominent area of interest. And the concept of a second brain had caught my attention before I started noticing how popular personal knowledge management was becoming. These experiences made me curious about my own thinking process. How do I arrive at these ideas? Why do certain possibilities seem obvious to me before they become popular conversations? I don't have a definitive answer. I just know that I tend to question existing approaches and imagine how they could work differently. Intuition Is the Starting Point, Not the Proof I don't believe every gut feeling is correct. An idea feeling right doesn't make it true. And thinking of something early doesn't automatically mean the idea is original or that it will succeed. That's why verification matters to me. When an idea catches my attention, I want to investigate it, understand the surrounding developments, and see whether there's a reasonable basis for believing it could happen. My process is simple: Intuition → Investigation → Verification → Prediction. The intuition gives me a direction to explore. Verification helps me determine whether that direction deserves attention. Sometimes the evidence supports the idea. Sometimes it changes my perspective. That's part of the process. I Think About What Could Exist, Not Just What Exists As someone interested in building products, I naturally think about possibilities. Could this workflow be simpler? Could two existing technologies work better together? What if we approached this problem from a completely different direction? Could the interface adapt to the user's needs instead of forcing the user to adapt to the interface? These questions often lead me toward ideas that aren't yet mainstream. I suspect this comes partly from thinking about products as systems rather than isolated features. When you consider how technology, user behavior, and existing limitations interact, you start seeing alternative possibilities. But seeing a possibility and making it useful are two very different things. The real challenge is determining which possibilities deserve to become products. Why I Want to Be Known as a Builder I could spend my time publishing predictions and discussing what the future might look like. But that's not the professional identity I want to cultivate. I want to build. I want to experiment with ideas, write code, explore architectures, create products, and discover what works by actually implementing it. Predictions are interesting, but building gives those ideas a practical test. A concept might sound compelling until you try to implement it. A product might appear unnecessary until someone uses it and discovers its value. Execution introduces constraints that imagination alone cannot reveal. That's why I want my work to speak louder than my predictions. I'd rather demonstrate an idea through a working prototype than repeatedly explain why I think it matters. Having Ideas Is Easy. Choosing What to Build Is Hard. I have more ideas than I can realistically pursue. Time is the constraint. Every interesting possibility competes with the time required to investigate it, build it, and determine whether it solves a real problem. I've realized that I don't need to execute every idea I have. I need to become better at identifying which ideas deserve my attention. Some ideas belong in a notebook. Some deserve further investigation. A few might justify building a prototype. And only a small number will be worth turning into actual products. The goal isn't to chase every possibility. It's to develop the judgment to choose wisely. So, How Do I Predict the Future? I wouldn't claim to know the future. What I can describe is how I approach possibilities before they become obvious to everyone around me. I start with intuition. I investigate the idea. I look for evidence. I form a view about what might happen. Sometimes that view may be early. Sometimes it may be wrong. I'm interested in improving the process rather than pretending it's infallible. I've noticed something interesting about the way I think about technology.

Sometimes, I get a gut feeling about how something should work, how a product could evolve, or how people's relationship with technology might change.

I don't always have a detailed explanation for it immediately. Sometimes, it's just an idea that feels worth exploring.

But I don't stop at the feeling.

I follow my intuition with verification.

It Starts With a Gut Feeling

Some ideas arrive before I have consciously analyzed every detail.

Before AI-assisted interviews became a widely discussed topic, I supported the idea that candidates should be allowed to use AI during interviews.

I had also explored the idea of modular, pluggable user interfaces before intelligent UIs became a more prominent area of interest.

And the concept of a second brain had caught my attention before I started noticing how popular personal knowledge management was becoming.

These experiences made me curious about my own thinking process.

How do I arrive at these ideas? Why do certain possibilities seem obvious to me before they become popular conversations?

I don't have a definitive answer.

I just know that I tend to question existing approaches and imagine how they could work differently.

Intuition Is the Starting Point, Not the Proof

I don't believe every gut feeling is correct.

An idea feeling right doesn't make it true. And thinking of something early doesn't automatically mean the idea is original or that it will succeed.

That's why verification matters to me.

When an idea catches my attention, I want to investigate it, understand the surrounding developments, and see whether there's a reasonable basis for believing it could happen.

My process is simple:

Intuition → Investigation → Verification → Prediction.

The intuition gives me a direction to explore. Verification helps me determine whether that direction deserves attention.

Sometimes the evidence supports the idea. Sometimes it changes my perspective.

That's part of the process.

I Think About What Could Exist, Not Just What Exists

As someone interested in building products, I naturally think about possibilities.

Could this workflow be simpler?

Could two existing technologies work better together?

What if we approached this problem from a completely different direction?

Could the interface adapt to the user's needs instead of forcing the user to adapt to the interface?

These questions often lead me toward ideas that aren't yet mainstream.

I suspect this comes partly from thinking about products as systems rather than isolated features. When you consider how technology, user behavior, and existing limitations interact, you start seeing alternative possibilities.

But seeing a possibility and making it useful are two very different things.

The real challenge is determining which possibilities deserve to become products.

Why I Want to Be Known as a Builder

I could spend my time publishing predictions and discussing what the future might look like.

But that's not the professional identity I want to cultivate.

I want to build.

I want to experiment with ideas, write code, explore architectures, create products, and discover what works by actually implementing it.

Predictions are interesting, but building gives those ideas a practical test.

A concept might sound compelling until you try to implement it. A product might appear unnecessary until someone uses it and discovers its value.

Execution introduces constraints that imagination alone cannot reveal.

That's why I want my work to speak louder than my predictions.

I'd rather demonstrate an idea through a working prototype than repeatedly explain why I think it matters.

I have more ideas than I can realistically pursue.

Time is the constraint.

Every interesting possibility competes with the time required to investigate it, build it, and determine whether it solves a real problem.

I've realized that I don't need to execute every idea I have. I need to become better at identifying which ideas deserve my attention.

The goal isn't to chase every possibility. It's to develop the judgment to choose wisely.

Anthropic's own docs spell out what that has meant until now: "one end customer can trigger an enforcement action that applies to your whole organization" ( Anthropic, user profiles ). On October 20, Anthropic shipped the fix: user profiles , so you can tell it which end customer each API request is for. On October 21 it added enforcement_status and enforcement_actions fields, so you can see whether Anthropic has restricted or banned one of your customers ( release notes ). MIXED News summed it up as resellers being able to get "one customer banned instead of their whole account." There's a catch in the fine print. The webhook that's supposed to tell you when a customer gets banned exists, takes registrations, and sends nothing. Anthropic's docs say so in a note: "Event delivery isn't live" ( organization webhooks ). What a user profile is A profile is a record you create once per end customer with POST /v1/user_profiles . It returns an ID that starts with uprof_ , and you send that ID in the anthropic-user-profile-id header on every request you make for that customer ( docs ). When a safety action hits that profile, "the rest of your traffic is unaffected," per the same page. Two details make it easy to adopt: Profiles "aren't billable and don't affect pricing" ( docs ). A profile doesn't contain conversation content, and Anthropic doesn't verify the details you send ( docs ). Who gets a profile depends on what you sell. A signed-up user of your app gets an application profile, the default. A company you resell API access to gets one passthrough profile for the whole company, not one per employee ( docs ). A request with no profile ID counts as your own usage, and Anthropic recommends keeping that usage in a separate organization, because profiles belong to an organization, not a workspace ( docs ). The SDKs take the ID as an argument. This is the Python call from Anthropic's page, with the import and the stored ID added and the print removed: import anthropic profile_id = " uprof_... " # the ID you stored at signup client = anthropic . Anthropic () message = client . messages . create ( model = " claude-opus-5-5 " , max_tokens = 1024 , messages = [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " Hello, Claude " }], user_profile_id = profile_id , ) The same header works on token counting, Message Batches and the OpenAI SDK compatibility endpoint ( docs ). "Every call creates a new profile, even when reference_id matches an existing one" ( docs ). Create it in your onboarding flow, store the uprof_ ID on the customer record, and have every service read it from there. A worker that calls create on startup will mint a new profile per boot. 2. An old beta header hides the ban fields. Responses leave out enforcement_status and enforcement_actions when your anthropic-beta header carries user-profiles-2026-09-04 or an earlier value, and the enforcement_status[] list filter returns a 400 ( webhooks docs ). Then comes the note: "Anthropic doesn't send the two events, so an endpoint you register receives nothing" ( docs ). You can build the handler today. You can't rely on it today. The enforcement webhook is wired to nothing for now. A scheduled check is the doorbell that works. items.title: Claude Code Automation: Publish Gates Blocked 23 Bad Posts in 10 Days
items.summary: If Claude Code runs anything that publishes, posts, or deletes for you, don't rely on a prompt that says "be careful." Put a small script between the model and the irreversible step, and make that script read the actual output. In 10 days (2026-09-28 to 2026-10-07) one such gate ran 248 times on my Claude Code-run blog pipeline and blocked 37 of those runs. That stopped 23 different posts before they went live. None of those numbers come from a model's "done!" message. They come from append-only JSON ledgers that every script writes on every run. Below are the counts, the four failures that forced each rule, and the steps to copy. The longer write-up, with the full tables, is on the original post . What I measured in 10 days Claude Code writes and edits the Python scripts, a Windows scheduler runs them, and each script appends one JSON line per run under data/ops/ . I counted the ledgers line by line on 2026-10-07. Measure Value Gate runs (247 Tistory, 1 dev.to) 248 Passed (exit 0) 206 Blocked (exit 1, defect found) 37 Checker itself broke (exit 2) 5 Distinct posts checked 57 Posts blocked at least once 23 Blocked, later fixed and passed 11 Over a longer window, 49 days with runs, the scheduled jobs logged 1,243 unattended runs across 44 jobs. 997 reported success with output, 207 reported success with zero output, and 39 reported failure. Why the gate blocked posts One run can carry two defects, so the reasons add up to 38 across the 37 blocked runs: kw-demand (21): the keyword-demand research file was missing or older than 45 days. fig-embed (6): charts were rendered but never inserted into the post body. rel-date (4): relative dates like "this weekend" that turn false if publishing slips a day. kw-grade (3): the target keyword was below the 200 monthly-search bar. fig-numbers (3): a number in a chart appeared nowhere in the post text. fig-count (1): fewer than 2 charts in the post. Most blocks are boring. That is the point: they are the cheap, mechanical mistakes a model will make while reporting that everything is fine. The 4 failures that created the rules Every gate exists because something went wrong while every check said fine. 1. 132 posts shipped with zero images. The pipeline had published 132 posts with no images in the body, and every verification run passed. The check looked at the social preview image and exempted any post that had one. The fix was a shared gate that counts charts actually embedded in the body, which is where fig-embed and fig-count come from. 2. A post went live, then the job crashed before writing its ledger. The daily job published at 05:01:20 and died at 05:03 with ValueError: I/O operation on closed file . A late import replaced sys.stdout with a new wrapper, the old wrapper was garbage-collected, and it closed the shared buffer. No ledger entry meant the next morning's run would have published the same post again. The fix: use sys.stdout.reconfigure(...) instead, and write the ledger line immediately after each publish rather than at the end of the batch. 3. A --dry run rewrote an input file. A dry run of a social-follow script overwrote its target list with 30 candidates the owner had already rejected. The next scheduled run would have followed them, and dev.to has no unfollow API. The rule: dry means no state changes, not "different output." If a dry path writes even one file, it is not dry. 4. Code pasted through a shell heredoc broke the publisher twice. \n inside an f-string became a real newline, which was a SyntaxError. Worse, \b in a regex became the 0x08 control character, so the image counter always returned 0. That one passed syntax checks and surfaced only as "2 charts inserted, 0 images counted." Now any code containing backslashes goes through the file-edit tool, and a control-character scan runs afterward. Why gates work where prompts don't A prompt like "verify your work" asks the model to grade itself. Claude Code is good at writing a checker, but it is not a reliable witness to its own run, because the run's log and the run's result can disagree. Failure 2 is exactly that: the post existed and the record of it didn't. A gate separates the two. It opens the output (the HTML, the chart files, the ledger) and returns an exit code, and the publisher refuses to continue on a defect. Claude Code then has a concrete, machine-readable reason to fix something. Of the 23 stopped posts, 11 were fixed and re-passed; the other 12 never passed in this window, so they never went out through the publisher with the defect. Copy this setup Give every checker three exit codes. 0 is clean, 1 is a defect, 2 means the checker itself is broken (no targets found, file unreadable). Finding zero things to check is exit 2, not a pass. Append one JSON line per run with timestamp, target, exit code, and defect names. If the line count doesn't grow, the check didn't run. Make the publish step call the gate and stop on exit 1. Put it inside the publisher, not in a checklist someone has to remember. Write the ledger the moment the irreversible action happens , not at the end of the batch. Restrict what a completion report may say. In CLAUDE.md , a report can cite only the checker's name and exit code, what a human actually opened, and what the gate cannot see. Log every failure as symptom, cause, fix , then turn the fix into a check. My 169 incident entries are where most gate rules came from. A minimal skeleton with the three exit codes and the ledger line: import json , sys , time from pathlib import Path def check ( html_path : Path ) -> list [ str ]: html = html_path . read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ) defects = [] if html . count ( " " ) < 2 : defects . append ( " fig-count " ) return defects def main ( paths : list [ str ]) -> int : targets = [ Path ( p ) for p in paths if Path ( p ). is_file ()] if not targets : return 2 # nothing to check means the checker is broken worst = 0 with open ( " gate.jsonl " , " a " , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as ledger : for t in targets : defects = check ( t ) code = 1 if defects else 0 worst = max ( worst , code ) ledger . write ( json . dumps ({ " ts " : time . strftime ( " %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S " ), " target " : str ( t ), " exit " : code , " defects " : defects , }) + " \n " ) return worst if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ( sys . argv [ 1 :])) The publish step then runs this and aborts when the exit code is not 0. Limits worth knowing A gate with bad measurement lies with confidence. The first live run of a page checker flagged 320 defects across 80 pages. Every one was an analytics beacon failing because the checker opened pages from file:// . When every target fails the same way, suspect the gate first. Gates see surface patterns, not quality. A title-hook detector rated a good title as having zero hooks because its word list was incomplete, and it blocked a publish. Expect false positives and keep an explicit override. "Success with zero output" is ambiguous. 207 runs reported success and produced nothing. Most were legitimate, such as a comment watcher with no new comments, so you must define per job what empty means. This is one operator's setup, a single blog platform over a few weeks. It shows the mechanism works here; it is not a benchmark. You don't need 44 jobs to start. Wrap the one script that publishes, posts, or deletes with a checker that exits 1 on the defect you fear most, and ask Claude Code to append a JSON line per run. For the full ledger tables and the incident details, read the full post on my-blog.org . Free tools I keep on my own site: 34 calculators and how-to guides - loans, severance pay, take-home salary, savings vs deposits. New ones go out in one email, no ads.

  • kw-grade (3): the target keyword was below the 200 monthly-search bar.
  • fig-numbers (3): a number in a chart appeared nowhere in the post text.
  • fig-count (1): fewer than 2 charts in the post.

Most blocks are boring. That is the point: they are the cheap, mechanical mistakes a model will make while reporting that everything is fine.

The 4 failures that created the rules

Every gate exists because something went wrong while every check said fine.

1. 132 posts shipped with zero images. The pipeline had published 132 posts with no images in the body, and every verification run passed. The check looked at the social preview image and exempted any post that had one. The fix was a shared gate that counts charts actually embedded in the body, which is where fig-embed and fig-count come from.

2. A post went live, then the job crashed before writing its ledger. The daily job published at 05:01:20 and died at 05:03 with ValueError: I/O operation on closed file. A late import replaced sys.stdout with a new wrapper, the old wrapper was garbage-collected, and it closed the shared buffer. No ledger entry meant the next morning's run would have published the same post again. The fix: use sys.stdout.reconfigure(...) instead, and write the ledger line immediately after each publish rather than at the end of the batch.

3. A --dry run rewrote an input file. A dry run of a social-follow script overwrote its target list with 30 candidates the owner had already rejected. The next scheduled run would have followed them, and dev.to has no unfollow API. The rule: dry means no state changes, not "different output." If a dry path writes even one file, it is not dry.

4. Code pasted through a shell heredoc broke the publisher twice. \n inside an f-string became a real newline, which was a SyntaxError. Worse, \b in a regex became the 0x08 control character, so the image counter always returned 0. That one passed syntax checks and surfaced only as "2 charts inserted, 0 images counted." Now any code containing backslashes goes through the file-edit tool, and a control-character scan runs afterward.

Why gates work where prompts don't

A prompt like "verify your work" asks the model to grade itself. Claude Code is good at writing a checker, but it is not a reliable witness to its own run, because the run's log and the run's result can disagree. Failure 2 is exactly that: the post existed and the record of it didn't.

A gate separates the two. It opens the output (the HTML, the chart files, the ledger) and returns an exit code, and the publisher refuses to continue on a defect. Claude Code then has a concrete, machine-readable reason to fix something. Of the 23 stopped posts, 11 were fixed and re-passed; the other 12 never passed in this window, so they never went out through the publisher with the defect.

Copy this setup
  1. Give every checker three exit codes. 0 is clean, 1 is a defect, 2 means the checker itself is broken (no targets found, file unreadable). Finding zero things to check is exit 2, not a pass.
  2. Append one JSON line per run with timestamp, target, exit code, and defect names. If the line count doesn't grow, the check didn't run.
  3. Make the publish step call the gate and stop on exit 1. Put it inside the publisher, not in a checklist someone has to remember.
  4. Write the ledger the moment the irreversible action happens, not at the end of the batch.
  5. Restrict what a completion report may say. In CLAUDE.md, a report can cite only the checker's name and exit code, what a human actually opened, and what the gate cannot see.
  6. Log every failure as symptom, cause, fix, then turn the fix into a check. My 169 incident entries are where most gate rules came from.

A minimal skeleton with the three exit codes and the ledger line:

import json, sys, time
from pathlib import Path

def check(html_path: Path) -> list[str]:
    html = html_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    defects = []
    if html.count("") < 2:
        defects.append("fig-count")
    return defects

def main(paths: list[str]) -> int:
    targets = [Path(p) for p in paths if Path(p).is_file()]
    if not targets:
        return 2  # nothing to check means the checker is broken
    worst = 0
    with open("gate.jsonl", "a", encoding="utf-8") as ledger:
        for t in targets:
            defects = check(t)
            code = 1 if defects else 0
            worst = max(worst, code)
            ledger.write(json.dumps({
                "ts": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
                "target": str(t), "exit": code, "defects": defects,
            }) + "\n")
    return worst

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

The publish step then runs this and aborts when the exit code is not 0.

Limits worth knowing
  • A gate with bad measurement lies with confidence. The first live run of a page checker flagged 320 defects across 80 pages. Every one was an analytics beacon failing because the checker opened pages from file://. When every target fails the same way, suspect the gate first.
  • Gates see surface patterns, not quality. A title-hook detector rated a good title as having zero hooks because its word list was incomplete, and it blocked a publish. Expect false positives and keep an explicit override.
  • "Success with zero output" is ambiguous. 207 runs reported success and produced nothing. Most were legitimate, such as a comment watcher with no new comments, so you must define per job what empty means.
  • This is one operator's setup, a single blog platform over a few weeks. It shows the mechanism works here; it is not a benchmark.

You don't need 44 jobs to start. Wrap the one script that publishes, posts, or deletes with a checker that exits 1 on the defect you fear most, and ask Claude Code to append a JSON line per run. For the full ledger tables and the incident details, read the full post on my-blog.org.

The most confusing Claude API failure is not a 400, a 429, or a 529. It is an HTTP 200 with an empty text block. Nothing was thrown and nothing was logged as an error, yet your JSON parser reports "no JSON found". In our case the cause was thinking tokens eating the whole max_tokens budget: 4,474 of 5,369 output tokens went to thinking, which left 895 for the answer.

This post is the triage order we use now. It separates "retry", "fix the request", and "wait", and it catches the failures that never produce an error at all. The longer write-up, with the full status table, is on the original post.

Errors share one shape, so classify by type

Every API error comes back as the same JSON object: a top-level error with a type and a message, plus a request_id.

{
  "type": "error",
  "error": {
    "type": "rate_limit_error",
    "message": "..."
  },
  "request_id": "req_..."
}

Branch on error.type, never on the message text. The docs say wording can change, and the SDK raises a different exception class per status code, so catch the class. A string comparison on the message will break silently one day.

The first-pass reading:

  • 400 (invalid_request_error): the request is wrong. Retrying the same request gives the same result.
  • 429 (rate_limit_error): a limit of some kind. Which kind matters, see the next section.
  • 529 (overloaded_error): temporary overload across all users. Wait and retry. It is not an account problem.
  • 500 (api_error) and 504 (timeout_error): server-side. Back off, or move long requests to streaming or the batch API.

One more detail: the SDK already retries connection errors, 429s, and 5xx responses twice with exponential backoff, honoring retry-after. If an exception reached your code, two more attempts already happened.

429 is three different problems

A 429 can be a rate limit, a monthly spend cap for your usage tier, or a Claude Code workspace spend limit. Only the first one clears if you wait.

The tell is the retry-after header. A rate limit sends it. A spend cap does not, and it keeps failing until access reopens. If you treat a spend cap as a rate limit and add backoff, you get a loop that receives the same 429 all day.

import anthropic

def classify_429(err: anthropic.RateLimitError) -> str:
    ra = err.response.headers.get("retry-after")
    if ra is None:
        return "cap-type: stop retrying, check spend caps and workspace limits"
    return f"rate-type: retry after {ra}s"

Rarely, a sudden jump in organization usage can trigger a 429 from an acceleration limit. The fix there is to ramp traffic up gradually and keep usage patterns even.

A 400 on a valid-looking request

When the payload looks fine, check whether the model dropped a parameter. These are the messages that mattered to us:

Message fragment Cause Fix "does not support assistant message prefill" Newer models reject a prefilled last assistant message Use structured output or the system prompt "thinking.type.enabled" is not supported Fixed budget_tokens thinking was removed on newer models thinking: {type: "adaptive"} plus effort "thinking blocks ... cannot be modified" You edited or dropped the previous assistant turn's thinking blocks Send them back unchanged tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported Some models reject forced tool calls auto plus strict tool use

One observation that is not in the official error docs: our LLM wrapper has a comment saying not to pass temperature, left behind after an old example that included it returned a 400. Treat that as our environment's experience, not a documented rule.

Empty response, HTTP 200, no error

Thinking tokens count toward max_tokens. If thinking spends the budget first, the response ends with stop_reason: "max_tokens" and the text block is truncated or missing. The status is 200 and no exception is raised.

Our case: a call asking for a content plan as JSON returned an empty string and failed with "JSON not found". We then walked a four-step misdiagnosis:

  1. The log said "JSON parse failed".
  2. We assumed the prompt was steering the model wrong and rewrote it.
  3. The same failure came back. It failed three times in a row.
  4. The real cause was the output budget. The clue was that the raw response was an empty string.

That last point is the discriminator. If the prompt had pushed the model toward prose instead of JSON, the raw response would not be empty. Only an empty raw string supports the "thinking used the budget" diagnosis.

def diagnose_empty(resp) -> str | None:
    text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
    if text.strip():
        return None
    thinking = getattr(getattr(resp.usage, "output_tokens_details", None),
                       "thinking_tokens", None)
    return (f"empty response: stop_reason={resp.stop_reason}, "
            f"output={resp.usage.output_tokens}, thinking={thinking}")

The field to read is usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens. When streaming, it only appears on the final message_delta event.

There are two official fixes: raise max_tokens so thinking and text both fit, or lower effort so thinking spends less. We added a third. We cut what a single call has to produce: instead of "plan N posts at once", we ask for one outline, then one table of contents per post. The call that had failed three times passed on the first try.

The rule of thumb: if the output must arrive in one piece, use the official fixes. If it can be split, split it.

A six-step check order
  1. Is the status 200? If the result is empty, it is an output budget problem. Read stop_reason and thinking_tokens.
  2. Is it a 400? Find the parameter name in the message (prefill, thinking.type, tool_choice). Do not retry unchanged.
  3. Is it a 429? retry-after present means rate-type; absent means cap-type, so stop the loop.
  4. Is it a 529 or 500? The SDK already retried twice. Wait longer, and record the request_id if it persists. Give that ID to support.
  5. Is it a 504 or a long request? Move anything that may exceed ten minutes to streaming or the batch API. Note that an error can still arrive after a streamed 200.
  6. Is it a Claude Code MCP tool? Check /mcp, and if only the first call fails, raise MCP_TIMEOUT.
When the first MCP call fails

If a Claude Code MCP tool fails only on its first call in a session, suspect a cold start. One of our search-console servers times out on the first call and works once a lightweight tool has woken it.

Control What it adjusts Example MCP_TIMEOUT env var Server startup wait MCP_TIMEOUT=10000 claude Per-server timeout in .mcp.json Tool execution time in ms "timeout": 600000 MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS Tool output token cap Default 25,000

The caution that matters most: do not retry a timed-out write. A timeout means "result unknown", not "failed". Resending a write that already landed applies the change twice, so check whether it took effect first.

Two things this table does not cover. The subscription limit messages in the Claude Code UI, such as "You've hit your session limit", are plan notices, not HTTP errors. And any automation that reports "success" while producing nothing belongs to the same family as the empty response.

items.title: AI Can Be Cyborg or Centaur. But Can Enterprises Monetise It?
items.summary: "Just because you consume tokens doesn't automatically mean there is a bank and you can start having a teller to withdraw money." That is how Satish Viswanathan sums up the thinking that took hold in 2024, when companies began treating token consumption as "a medal" of their AI capabilities. Some organisations even specified token consumption commitments in hiring packages. Two years later, companies are beginning to recognise that consuming tokens without any checks costs money without necessarily generating revenue. Viswanathan, the former global data and AI lead for travel at Accenture, is the author of The Weight of Intelligence . In an interview on Front Page with AIM Network, he argues that businesses are focusing too much on improving AI models and too little on their ability to absorb and use the technology. He calls this challenge "enterprise metabolisation". Having access to increasingly capable AI models does not automatically make an organisation more productive or profitable. Companies also need the people, processes, and infrastructure to put that intelligence to work. The Enterprise Adoption Problem Viswanathan identifies several factors that determine how effectively an enterprise can use AI : model capability, enterprise data architecture and availability, system integration and infrastructure, human processes and organisational structures, value economics, and governance and regulation. Every enterprise, he argues, has its own "technology debt, people debt, process debt" and organisational-structure debt. These constraints determine how much of a model's intelligence a company can actually use. Even access to artificial general intelligence (AGI), he believes, would not make every enterprise equally capable. "Still, every enterprise is unique." Companies cannot assume that the same technology will produce the same results everywhere. For business leaders, this means looking beyond the capabilities of AI models and examining whether their organisations can put those capabilities to productive use. Token consumption may show that employees are using AI, but it does not establish whether the technology is generating revenue or reducing costs. Measuring Financial Returns Viswanathan sees a shift in how companies approach AI projects. Competitive pressure and vendor partnerships are becoming strong tailwinds. He has also observed a pause in enterprise AI adoption . Companies are not necessarily abandoning the technology, but some are pursuing fewer use cases at once and reconsidering the scale of their investments. "We've already seen very, very smart pausing," he says, describing how some enterprises are containing their spending rather than going "full throttle". He linked this reassessment to pressure on chief executives to demonstrate returns from AI spending. As he put it, companies still need to figure out "what is the use case, what is the area of intervention and how to make money out of it". Productivity Gains are Not Savings Even when AI makes a task faster, the time saved does not automatically become a financial gain for the company. Viswanathan illustrates this with an employee who saves an hour by using AI to complete a task. The employee could, for instance, use that time for a yoga class. "We are not in this factory model where the moment we go at 9 am when you punch your card, you're invariably working," he notes. Knowledge workers do not necessarily spend every hour on assigned tasks, and time freed up by AI may not automatically be redirected to other work. The financial benefit depends on what the organisation does with that time. Companies need to encourage employees to use it productively, potentially by giving them new responsibilities or helping them develop additional skills. The same challenge applies to technology services companies. If AI allows a provider to complete work faster, clients may expect the resulting efficiency gains to be reflected in contract prices. The provider may therefore be unable to retain all the savings. Risks of Automation The pressure to improve efficiency also raises questions about how companies develop their workforce. Viswanathan warned that reducing entry-level hiring because AI can perform routine tasks could create problems over time. Employees build institutional knowledge through years of working on projects, observing decisions, and learning from failures. That experience helps prepare them for more senior responsibilities. "If you restrict people joining at the bottom of the pyramid, it's a disaster in the long term," he remarks. He acknowledges that reducing entry-level hiring could improve operating margins in the short term. However, companies risk weakening the pipeline through which employees acquire the experience needed to advance. As AI becomes part of everyday work, organisations must also decide how people and AI systems should share responsibilities. Referring to a Harvard study from roughly two years ago, Viswanathan describes two models of human-AI collaboration: the "cyborg" and the "centaur". In the cyborg model, human and AI contributions are intertwined, making it difficult to distinguish where one ends and the other begins. In the centaur model, responsibilities are divided more clearly between people and algorithms. Limits of Autonomous AI The question of human judgement becomes more important as companies adopt AI agents that can perform tasks with limited intervention. Viswanathan questions how readily businesses use the term "autonomous" to describe AI systems. Even experienced employees, he observes, seek a second opinion before making major decisions. Employees often consult colleagues or managers before acting. Having a human in the loop does not, by itself, solve the problem. Viswanathan describes human oversight as "your last resort". A person cannot realistically monitor thousands of agents or millions of interactions individually. Instead, he argues, enterprises will need observation models that monitor AI interactions, identify anomalies, and escalate relevant cases to people. "Otherwise, just saying ‘ human in the loop ’ means then you have to get more humans," he comments. That, he argues, could defeat the return-on-investment case for deploying AI in the first place. Redesigning Enterprises for AI Viswanathan's proposed response is to rethink how organisations make decisions and carry out work. He calls this approach "enterprise cognition", in which humans and AI jointly make decisions, with people retaining leadership and AI providing support. He does not advocate replacing an entire operating model at once. Instead, he favours an incremental transition wherein companies redesign one process or business unit at a time before extending the changes across the organisation. He cautions that simply adding AI to existing processes would not necessarily produce the financial impact companies expect. "If you're just doing ad hoc use cases... ad hoc processes being picked up and just AI-fied, you're not going to have that net P&L impact which we are hoping to have," he explains. The challenge for the leadership is understanding how AI can be incorporated into organisational decision-making and how those changes affect business performance. India's Opportunity Viswanathan believes India could strengthen its position in enterprise AI by drawing on its experience in technology services and systems integration. Achieving this, however, will require changes in education and research. Training programmes often focus on building AI solutions, he says. Enterprises also need people who can understand how to integrate those solutions into business operations and connect them to commercial outcomes. He calls for more research focused on practical industry problems. He also proposes an open-source ecosystem in which organisations could share knowledge and learn from one another while retaining ownership of their intellectual property. For India's global capability centres (GCCs), Viswanathan says the focus should shift from headcount to their economic contribution to the parent organisation's profit and loss. He wants India to become a centre for enterprise AI return on investment, helping companies translate AI capabilities into business value. He also highlights the importance of preserving human judgement as AI becomes more deeply embedded in work. In some situations, he suggests, organisations may deliberately limit AI use to help employees retain their critical-thinking skills.

Viswanathan warned that reducing entry-level hiring because AI can perform routine tasks could create problems over time. Employees build institutional knowledge through years of working on projects, observing decisions, and learning from failures. That experience helps prepare them for more senior responsibilities.

"If you restrict people joining at the bottom of the pyramid, it's a disaster in the long term," he remarks.

He acknowledges that reducing entry-level hiring could improve operating margins in the short term. However, companies risk weakening the pipeline through which employees acquire the experience needed to advance.

As AI becomes part of everyday work, organisations must also decide how people and AI systems should share responsibilities. Referring to a Harvard study from roughly two years ago, Viswanathan describes two models of human-AI collaboration: the "cyborg" and the "centaur".

In the cyborg model, human and AI contributions are intertwined, making it difficult to distinguish where one ends and the other begins. In the centaur model, responsibilities are divided more clearly between people and algorithms.

Limits of Autonomous AI

The question of human judgement becomes more important as companies adopt AI agents that can perform tasks with limited intervention.

Viswanathan questions how readily businesses use the term "autonomous" to describe AI systems. Even experienced employees, he observes, seek a second opinion before making major decisions. Employees often consult colleagues or managers before acting.

Having a human in the loop does not, by itself, solve the problem. Viswanathan describes human oversight as "your last resort". A person cannot realistically monitor thousands of agents or millions of interactions individually. 

Instead, he argues, enterprises will need observation models that monitor AI interactions, identify anomalies, and escalate relevant cases to people. 

"Otherwise, just saying ‘human in the loop’ means then you have to get more humans," he comments. That, he argues, could defeat the return-on-investment case for deploying AI in the first place.

Redesigning Enterprises for AI

Viswanathan's proposed response is to rethink how organisations make decisions and carry out work. He calls this approach "enterprise cognition", in which humans and AI jointly make decisions, with people retaining leadership and AI providing support.

He does not advocate replacing an entire operating model at once. Instead, he favours an incremental transition wherein companies redesign one process or business unit at a time before extending the changes across the organisation.

He cautions that simply adding AI to existing processes would not necessarily produce the financial impact companies expect. "If you're just doing ad hoc use cases... ad hoc processes being picked up and just AI-fied, you're not going to have that net P&L impact which we are hoping to have," he explains.

The challenge for the leadership is understanding how AI can be incorporated into organisational decision-making and how those changes affect business performance. 

India's Opportunity

Viswanathan believes India could strengthen its position in enterprise AI by drawing on its experience in technology services and systems integration.

Achieving this, however, will require changes in education and research. Training programmes often focus on building AI solutions, he says. Enterprises also need people who can understand how to integrate those solutions into business operations and connect them to commercial outcomes.

He calls for more research focused on practical industry problems. He also proposes an open-source ecosystem in which organisations could share knowledge and learn from one another while retaining ownership of their intellectual property.

For India's global capability centres (GCCs), Viswanathan says the focus should shift from headcount to their economic contribution to the parent organisation's profit and loss. He wants India to become a centre for enterprise AI return on investment, helping companies translate AI capabilities into business value.

He also highlights the importance of preserving human judgement as AI becomes more deeply embedded in work. In some situations, he suggests, organisations may deliberately limit AI use to help employees retain their critical-thinking skills.

  • Worst: Validation is only as strong as your tests. Managed runtimes, appliances and Electron apps are flagged, not patched.
What is the Devin Vulnerability Fixes plugin?

The Devin Vulnerability Fixes plugin is a set of three Agent Skills from Cognition. They find and patch vulnerable PHP, Node.js and self-managed GitLab deployments. The source is on GitHub under the MIT license. Cognition’s product page lists it as free and open source.

Which vulnerabilities does it fix?
  • PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): PHP rates both flaws CVSS v4.0 9.2. The first corrupts memory after an out-of-memory condition. The second lets stale global state from one request reach the next. PHP says every web-serving setup is at risk, with mod_php rated highest risk. Fixed versions are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP 8.1 and older get no releases, only source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1.
  • Node.js October 2026 release: It fixes 10 CVEs, 4 rated High. The lead bug, CVE-2026-111497, is a Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write that can enable RCE. Fixed versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. Node.js 20 and older are end-of-life and get no fix.
  • GitLab CVE-2026-110264: An integer overflow in the regular expression compiler allows unauthenticated code execution. It affects GitLab CE/EE from 7.0 onward and scores CVSS 10.0. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched.
How does the plugin work?

Every skill follows the same five-step shape:

  1. Read-only inventory: The agent scans Dockerfiles, base images, distro packages, CI, Helm, Terraform, Packer, Lambda and config management.
  2. Approval gate: Nothing changes until you pick repos. Riskier minor or major upgrades are called out first.
  3. Verified target: Every tag, digest, package version and checksum is confirmed against the official source before editing.
  4. Test before and after: The suite runs on the current version, then inside the new production image. Regressions stop the run.
  5. One PR per repo: Each PR carries versions, test results, runtime diffs, a risk label and a rollback plan.

The skills also encode known patching traps. Debian and Ubuntu backport fixes without changing upstream versions, so php -v can mislead. Ubuntu 24.04’s fixed package is 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13. Digest-pinned images need a new digest. Changing Composer’s require.php patches nothing.

In Devin, open Customize, then Plugins, then Browse Marketplace, and search for Vulnerability Fixes. The Devin CLI uses devin plugins install CognitionAI/devin-marketplace#plugins/devin-vuln-fixes. For other agents, run npx skills add CognitionAI/devin-vuln-fixes. Claude Code users can add the marketplace and run /plugin install vuln-fixes@cognition-skills.

Then ask in plain language, such as ‘Please fix my PHP vulnerability.’ Slash commands also work: /fix-php-vuln, /fix-node-vuln and /fix-gitlab-vuln.

In this tutorial, we work with Underdog Saluki 27B, a 7.9 GB build of Qwen3.8-27B that its makers say keeps tool calling intact at about two bits per weight and even edges out the full 54 GB model on their own 120-task benchmark. Saluki is built on ISTA-DASLab’s GSQ-RCO quantization of the same model, so we put both files side by side in stock llama.cpp. We start with the files themselves: a tensor-by-tensor diff of the two GGUF headers, then a byte-level comparison that shows whether Saluki is a remix of ISTA’s bits or a changed model. We then serve each file on one GPU, read its memory and speed, and score both on the same seeded 120 tasks from the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, using BFCL’s own checker with strict and lenient parsing.

def read_gguf(path):
    """GGUF v3 header: metadata, tensor table (name, dims, type, offset) and where the tensor data starts."""
    f = open(path, "rb")
    u = lambda fmt: struct.unpack("<" + fmt, f.read(struct.calcsize(fmt)))[0]
    s = lambda: f.read(u("Q")).decode("utf-8", "replace")
    scalar = {0: "B", 1: "b", 2: "H", 3: "h", 4: "I", 5: "i", 6: "f", 7: "?", 10: "Q", 11: "q", 12: "d"}
 
    def val(t):
        if t == 8:
            return s()
        if t == 9:
            et, n = u("I"), u("Q")
            return [val(et) for _ in range(n)]
        return u(scalar[t])
    assert f.read(4) == b"GGUF"
    version, n_tensors, n_kv = u("I"), u("Q"), u("Q")
    kv = {}
    for _ in range(n_kv):
        k = s()
        kv[k] = val(u("I"))
    tensors = []
    for _ in range(n_tensors):
        name = s()
        dims = [u("Q") for _ in range(u("I"))]
        ttype, off = u("I"), u("Q")
        n = math.prod(dims)
        _, per, nbytes = GGML_TYPES[ttype]
        tensors.append(dict(name=name, dims=dims, type=GGML_TYPES[ttype][0], n=n, bytes=n // per * nbytes, off=off))
    align = kv.get("general.alignment", 32)
    data_start = (f.tell() + align - 1) // align * align
    return kv, tensors, data_start
 
 
 
def tensor_class(name):

Speed comes from the server’s own timings rather than a stopwatch around the request. We send a 256-token and a 1,024-token prompt with the prompt cache off and force 128 output tokens, which gives a prefill rate and a decode rate at each length. A dense 27B model reads its full weight file for every generated token, so decode speed mostly depends on memory bandwidth, and the same probe runs again on ISTA’s file later for a like-for-like comparison.

def load_bfcl_checker():
    """BFCL's own checker functions, executed from the pinned source with their package imports replaced."""
    src = lambda rel: open(os.path.join(WORK, "bfcl", rel.replace("/", "__"))).read()
 
    def run(rel, ns, only=None):
        tree = ast.parse(src(rel))
        body = [n for n in tree.body if not isinstance(n, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom))]
        if only:
            body = [n for n in body if getattr(n, "name", None) in only]
        exec(compile(ast.Module(body=body, type_ignores=[]), rel, "exec"), ns)
        return ns
    enums = run("constants/enums.py", {"Enum": enum.Enum})
    tmap = run("constants/type_mappings.py", {})
    model_cfg = collections.defaultdict(lambda: types.SimpleNamespace(underscore_to_dot=True))   # OpenAI-style FC model
    chk = run("eval_checker/ast_eval/ast_checker.py", {"re": re, "Language": enums["Language"], "MODEL_CONFIG_MAPPING": model_cfg,
              "JAVA_TYPE_CONVERSION": tmap["JAVA_TYPE_CONVERSION"], "JS_TYPE_CONVERSION": tmap["JS_TYPE_CONVERSION"],
              "java_type_converter": None, "js_type_converter": None})
    utl = run("utils.py", {}, {"is_function_calling_format_output", "is_empty_output"})
    conv = run("model_handler/utils.py", {"copy": copy, "re": re, "json": json, "ModelStyle": enums["ModelStyle"],
               "GORILLA_TO_OPENAPI": tmap["GORILLA_TO_OPENAPI"]}, {"_cast_to_openai_type", "convert_to_tool"})
    return types.SimpleNamespace(
        ast_checker=lambda funcs, out, gt, cat: chk["ast_checker"](funcs, out, gt, enums["Language"].PYTHON, cat, "fc-model"),
        is_empty=utl["is_empty_output"],
        to_tools=lambda funcs: conv["convert_to_tool"](funcs, tmap["GORILLA_TO_OPENAPI"], enums["ModelStyle"].OPENAI_COMPLETIONS))
 
 
def load_tasks():
    tasks = []
    for kind, label in KINDS:
        rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open(os.path.join(WORK, "bfcl", f"data__BFCL_v4_{kind}.json")) if l.strip()]
        gt = {}
        if kind != "irrelevance":
            for l in open(os.path.join(WORK, "bfcl", f"data__possible_answer__BFCL_v4_{kind}.json")):
                if l.strip():
                    d = json.loads(l); gt[d["id"]] = d["ground_truth"]
        for r in sorted(random.Random(f"{SEED}-{kind}").sample(rows, N_PER_KIND), key=lambda r: int(r["id"].rsplit("_", 1)[1])):
            tasks.append(dict(id=r["id"], kind=kind, messages=r["question"][0], functions=r["function"], gt=gt.get(r["id"])))
    return tasks
 
 
TOOL_BLOCK = re.compile(r"(.*?)(?:|$)", re.S)
FUNC_XML = re.compile(r"\s]+)\s*>(.*?)(?:|$)", re.S)
PARAM_XML = re.compile(r"\s]+)\s*>\n?(.*?)\n?", re.S)
 
 
def lenient_calls(raw, functions):
    """Forgiving reading of the model's raw text: any  block, closed or not, inside or outside .
    Values are typed with the function's own schema (BFCL types). Not part of BFCL; used only for the 'lenient' column."""
    raw = raw.split("")[-1]                    # with thinking on, the reasoning precedes 
    types_ = {re.sub(r"\.", "_", f["name"]): {k: v.get("type", "string") for k, v in f["parameters"]["properties"].items()}
              for f in functions}                       # tool names were sent with dots turned into underscores
    calls = []
    for fname, body in FUNC_XML.findall(raw):
        fname = fname.strip().strip('"')
        args = {}
        for p, v in PARAM_XML.findall(body):
            t = types_.get(re.sub(r"\.", "_", fname), {}).get(p, "string")
            v = v.strip() if t != "string" else v
            try:
                args[p] = (int(v) if t == "integer" else float(v) if t in ("float", "number") else
                           v.lower() == "true" if t == "boolean" and v.lower() in ("true", "false") else
                           json.loads(v) if t in ("array", "tuple", "dict", "object") else v)
            except ValueError:
                try:
                    args[p] = ast.literal_eval(v)
                except Exception:
                    args[p] = v
        calls.append({fname: args})
    return calls
 
 
def score(task, calls):
    """BFCL's rule: irrelevance passes with no call; the other kinds go through BFCL's ast_checker."""
    if task["kind"] == "irrelevance":
        return CHECK.is_empty(calls), "made a call" if calls else None
    if not calls:
        return False, "no call"
    try:
        r = CHECK.ast_checker(task["functions"], calls, task["gt"], task["kind"])
    except Exception as e:                       # malformed arguments the checker cannot walk
        return False, f"checker_error:{type(e).__name__}"
    return bool(r["valid"]), r.get("error_type")
 
 
def run_task(task, think=False, max_tokens=512):
    body = {"messages": task["messages"], "tools": CHECK.to_tools(task["functions"]), "max_tokens": max_tokens,
            "cache_prompt": False, "verbose": True, **GREEDY,
            "chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "low"} if think else {"enable_thinking": False}}
    log_pos = os.path.getsize(SERVER["log"])
    t0 = time.time()
    rec = dict(id=task["id"], kind=task["kind"], think=think)
    try:
        r = api("/v1/chat/completions", body)
        msg = r["choices"][0]["message"]
        rec.update(status=200, finish=r["choices"][0]["finish_reason"], raw=r["__verbose"]["content"],
                   prompt_n=r["timings"]["prompt_n"], out_n=r["timings"]["predicted_n"],
                   reasoning_chars=len(msg.get("reasoning_content") or ""))
        rec["calls"] = [{tc["function"]["name"]: json.loads(tc["function"]["arguments"])} for tc in msg.get("tool_calls") or []]
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:            # stock llama.cpp answers 500 when its parser cannot read the reply
        time.sleep(0.5)
        with open(SERVER["log"], errors="replace") as f:
            f.seek(log_pos)
            new = f.read()
        m = re.findall(r"=== BEGIN ===\n(.*?)\n=== END ===", new, re.S)
        rec.update(status=e.code, finish="parse error", raw=m[-1] if m else "", calls=None, prompt_n=None, out_n=None)
    rec["seconds"] = time.time() - t0
    rec["strict"], rec["strict_why"] = score(task, rec["calls"]) if rec["calls"] is not None else (False, "unparsed (HTTP 500)")
    if rec["strict"]:
        rec["lenient"] = True
    else:
        rec["lenient"], _ = score(task, lenient_calls(rec["raw"], task["functions"]))
    return rec
 
 
def bench(tag, tasks):
    out, t0 = [], time.time()
    for i, task in enumerate(tasks):
        out.append(run_task(task))
        if (i + 1) % 30 == 0:
            print(f"   {tag}: {i + 1}/{len(tasks)} done, {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
    json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(WORK, "runs", f"bfcl_{tag}.json"), "w"), indent=1)
    return out
 
 
def ci(k, n, alpha=0.05):
    """Clopper-Pearson interval by bisection on the binomial tail."""
    def cdf(x, p):
        return sum(math.comb(n, i) * p ** i * (1 - p) ** (n - i) for i in range(x + 1))
 
    def solve(f, target, rising):
        lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
        for _ in range(60):
            mid = (lo + hi) / 2
            lo, hi = (mid, hi) if (f(mid) < target) == rising else (lo, mid)
        return (lo + hi) / 2
    lo = 0.0 if k == 0 else solve(lambda p: 1 - cdf(k - 1, p), alpha / 2, True)
    hi = 1.0 if k == n else solve(lambda p: cdf(k, p), alpha / 2, False)
    return lo, hi
 
 
def kind_table(tag, recs):
    print(f"\n{tag}: {'kind':38s} {'strict':>8s} {'lenient':>8s}  replies: structured / plain text / unparsed (500) / cut off")
    for kind, label in KINDS:
        rs = [r for r in recs if r["kind"] == kind]
        st = collections.Counter("unparsed" if r["status"] != 200 else "cut off" if r["finish"] == "length"
                                 else "structured" if r["calls"] else "plain text" for r in rs)
        print(f"   {label:44s} {sum(r['strict'] for r in rs):3d}/{len(rs):<4d} {sum(r['lenient'] for r in rs):3d}/{len(rs):<4d}"
              f"  {st['structured']:3d} / {st['plain text']:3d} / {st['unparsed']:3d} / {st['cut off']:3d}")
    k, n = sum(r["strict"] for r in recs), len(recs)
    lo, hi = ci(k, n)
    print(f"   {'total':44s} {k:3d}/{n:<4d} {sum(r['lenient'] for r in recs):3d}/{n:<4d}  strict 95% CI {100 * lo:.0f}-{100 * hi:.0f}%")
 
 
@section("7. Tool calling on 120 BFCL v4 tasks, thinking off: Saluki")
def bench_saluki():
    global CHECK, TASKS, RUNS
    CHECK = load_bfcl_checker()
    TASKS = load_tasks()
    print(f"sample: {N_PER_KIND} tasks per kind, drawn with seed {SEED}, {len(TASKS)} in all; scored with BFCL's ast_checker "
          f"(gorilla@6ea5797); greedy, thinking off, max_tokens 512")
    print(f"first ids per kind: " + ", ".join(t["id"] for t in TASKS[::N_PER_KIND]))
    RUNS = {"Saluki": bench("Saluki", TASKS)}
    kind_table("Saluki", RUNS["Saluki"])
    sec = [r["seconds"] for r in RUNS["Saluki"]]
    print(f"\nmedian {sorted(sec)[len(sec) // 2]:.1f} s per task on {HW}; median output {sorted(r['out_n'] or 0 for r in RUNS['Saluki'])[len(sec) // 2]} tokens")
    again = [run_task(t) for t in TASKS[:: len(TASKS) // 5][:5]]
    same = sum(a["calls"] == b["calls"] and a["raw"] == b["raw"] for a, b in zip(again, RUNS["Saluki"][:: len(TASKS) // 5][:5]))
    print(f"greedy re-run of 5 tasks: {same} of 5 identical raw replies")
    claim("greedy decoding with the prompt cache off gives the same reply on a re-run (5 tasks)", same == 5)
    s = sum(r["strict"] for r in RUNS["Saluki"])
    return f"Saluki {s}/{len(TASKS)} strict, {sum(r['lenient'] for r in RUNS['Saluki'])}/{len(TASKS)} lenient"
 
 
bench_saluki()

Underdog Bench’s 120 tasks are not published, so we draw our own: 24 per kind from the same five BFCL v4 categories, with a fixed seed. We send each task to the server as an OpenAI tool request, converted with BFCL’s own function, with thinking off and greedy decoding. Strict scoring uses only the calls llama.cpp parses and BFCL’s ast_checker, while lenient scoring re-reads the raw reply with a forgiving parser, which is how we test the vendor’s strict-versus-forgiving gap.

thinking_step()

Turning thinking on is the card’s advice for general use, but at 27B every reasoning token costs time. We re-run six seeded multi-call tasks with reasoning on at the lowest effort and compare them with the same tasks run with thinking off: pass or fail, output tokens and seconds. Six tasks cannot settle whether thinking improves tool calls, so the cell focuses on cost and shows how many extra tokens a single tool call buys when the model thinks first.

The parent file follows the same path. We stop Saluki’s server, start one on ISTA’s IQ2_XS file with the same flags, read its memory, repeat the speed probe and score it on the same 120 tasks with the same checker and parsing rules. Running one model at a time keeps each well within the GPU’s memory, and using one harness for both removes differences in prompts, sampling, or parsing from the comparison.

def mcnemar(a, b):
    """Exact two-sided McNemar test on paired pass/fail lists."""
    b10 = sum(x and not y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    b01 = sum(y and not x for x, y in zip(a, b))
    n, k = b10 + b01, min(b10, b01)
    p = min(1.0, 2 * sum(math.comb(n, i) for i in range(k + 1)) / 2 ** n) if n else 1.0
    return b10, b01, p
 
 
@section("10. Head to head: the same 120 tasks, paired, next to the vendor's numbers")
def head_to_head():
    S, I = RUNS["Saluki"], RUNS["ISTA"]
    assert [r["id"] for r in S] == [r["id"] for r in I]
    vendor = {"simple_python": 24, "multiple": 23, "irrelevance": 18, "parallel": 12, "parallel_multiple": 11}
    print(f"{'kind':38s} {'Saluki':>7s} {'ISTA':>6s} | {'lenient':>7s} {'':>5s} | vendor's Saluki (of 24)")
    for kind, label in KINDS:
        s = [r for r in S if r["kind"] == kind]; i = [r for r in I if r["kind"] == kind]
        print(f"{label:38s} {sum(r['strict'] for r in s):7d} {sum(r['strict'] for r in i):6d} | "
              f"{sum(r['lenient'] for r in s):7d} {sum(r['lenient'] for r in i):5d} | {vendor[kind]:3d}")
    out = {}
    for mode in ("strict", "lenient"):
        a, b = [r[mode] for r in S], [r[mode] for r in I]
        b10, b01, p = mcnemar(a, b)
        out[mode] = (sum(a), sum(b), b10, b01, p)
        print(f"{mode:8s}: Saluki {sum(a)}/120, ISTA {sum(b)}/120; Saluki-only passes {b10}, ISTA-only {b01}, exact McNemar p = {p:.3f}")
    print("vendor's Underdog Bench (different 120 tasks, unpublished): Saluki 88, ISTA IQ2_XS 76, full Qwen3.8-27B 84")
    sa, ia, b10, b01, p = out["strict"]
    claim("Saluki passes more of our 120 tasks than its parent (strict scoring)", sa > ia)
    claim("the difference is significant at 5% (exact McNemar)", p < 0.05)
    pick_s = sum(r["strict"] for r in S if r["kind"] in ("simple_python", "multiple"))
    pick_i = sum(r["strict"] for r in I if r["kind"] in ("simple_python", "multiple"))
    claim("Saluki is at least as good as its parent at picking the right single function (first two kinds)", pick_s >= pick_i)
    return f"strict: Saluki {sa}/120 vs ISTA {ia}/120 (McNemar p = {p:.2f}); lenient: {out['lenient'][0]} vs {out['lenient'][1]}"

A gap of a few tasks in 120 sits inside run-to-run noise, as the vendor’s page itself concedes, so the test tells us whether our sample shows a real difference.

In conclusion, Saluki is not quite what its file suggests. Its header keeps ISTA’s 851-tensor layout and saves bits only where ISTA spent more, yet its bytes and unquantized vectors show a model whose weights were changed, consistent with Underdog calling it a preview checkpoint. That turns the tool-calling comparison with its parent into a test of that training rather than of quantization alone. Both files run in stock llama.cpp, one at a time, and BFCL’s own checker gives a paired comparison on identical tasks. Small samples, greedy decoding, and a single run limit what any one notebook can claim, so the intervals matter as much as the scores.
